description: How businesses recruit the right people and why training boosts retention.
content_html:
Why Recruitment Matters

Every business needs the right people in the right roles. Poor recruitment is expensive: advertising costs money, interviewing takes management time, and if the wrong person is hired, the business faces the cost of retraining or starting the process again. Getting recruitment right the first time saves time and money and improves the performance of the whole team.

Recruitment begins with a clear understanding of what the job involves and what kind of person would do it well. Two key documents make this explicit before a single application arrives.

Recruitment Documents

A job description sets out what the job involves: the job title, the department, who the employee will report to, the main duties, and the expected working hours. It tells applicants exactly what they would be doing if appointed.

Alongside the job description, a person specification details what the ideal candidate looks like. It lists essential requirements — the minimum a candidate must have to be considered — and desirable ones, which are advantages but not deal-breakers. For example, a person specification for an accounts assistant might list “GCSE Maths grade 5+” as essential and “experience with accounting software” as desirable.

Applicants respond using one of two routes. A standard application form allows the employer to collect information in a consistent format, making it easier to compare candidates fairly. Alternatively, some employers accept a CV (curriculum vitae), which the applicant prepares themselves. CVs give candidates more freedom to present their strengths but make direct comparison harder for employers.

Key Fact

A job description describes the role; a person specification describes the ideal candidate. Both are written before recruitment begins and guide every stage of the selection process, including shortlisting and interview questions.

Job Roles and Responsibilities

Businesses are structured around different levels of job role, each with distinct responsibilities. Directors sit at the top and set the strategy and vision of the company. Below them, senior managers translate that strategy into operational plans and lead major departments. Supervisors or team leaders manage front-line staff directly, monitoring output and resolving day-to-day issues. Operational and support staff carry out the practical work that delivers the product or service to customers.

Understanding these layers is important when recruiting: a vacancy at supervisor level requires a very different person specification from one at director level. Seniority determines pay, authority, and the expectations placed on the employee.

Internal and External Recruitment

Once documents are prepared, the business decides whether to recruit internally or externally. Internal recruitment promotes or transfers someone already working for the business. It is faster and cheaper than advertising externally, the candidate already understands the company’s culture, and it motivates other staff by showing that progression is possible. The disadvantage is that it leaves a gap elsewhere in the business and brings no new ideas or skills from outside.

External recruitment advertises the role to the public or through agencies, job boards, university careers fairs, or social media. It brings in fresh perspectives and new skills, and it is the only option when the business needs expertise it does not currently have. However, it is more expensive and time-consuming, and the employer takes on more risk because they know less about the new person than they would about an internal candidate.

The best method depends on the nature of the vacancy and the business’s situation. A rapidly growing technology business entering a new market might need external specialist knowledge that no existing employee can provide. By contrast, a stable business filling a supervisory role among experienced staff might get better results — and save significant cost — by promoting from within.

In practice, many businesses use both. They advertise internally first to give employees the opportunity to progress, then open the search externally if no internal candidate is strong enough. This balances motivation and cost against the need to bring in new capability.

Key Fact

Internal recruitment is cheaper and faster; external recruitment brings fresh skills and ideas. The choice depends on whether the business needs continuity or new capability, and how urgently the vacancy needs to be filled.

Training and Development

Recruiting well is only the first step. Businesses that invest in their employees through training and development see higher productivity, lower turnover, and a more skilled workforce. Training can take many forms depending on the employee’s role, the business’s budget, and the knowledge that needs to be transferred.

Formal training is planned and organised: it might be an off-the-job course, a workshop, or a qualification programme. A new receptionist attending a customer service course is an example of formal training. Informal training happens on the job without a structured programme — a junior employee watching an experienced colleague handle a complaint, for instance. Informal training is low-cost but less consistent in quality.

Beyond initial training, businesses use ongoing learning to keep staff up to date. Performance reviews are structured meetings in which manager and employee discuss targets, achievements, and development goals. They give employees clear feedback and allow the business to identify skill gaps before they become problems. Target-setting links individual employee goals to the wider business plan, providing direction and motivation.

There is a strong link between training and retention. Employees who feel they are developing their skills are more likely to stay with the business because they see a future there. High retention matters because replacing an employee costs money — advertising, interviewing, and induction all take time and resources — and experienced employees are more productive than new ones still learning the role.

Businesses also retrain employees when they introduce new technology. A manufacturing company upgrading its production line will need to train staff to use the new equipment safely and efficiently. Without retraining, productivity gains from the new technology may not be realised. This makes training a strategic investment rather than just an administrative task.
exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark Explain question about recruitment or training, the examiner marks only your best two points — so write two clear, well-developed points rather than trying to squeeze in three or four. A common error is to name a method (e.g. “external recruitment”) without explaining why it benefits the business or what its trade-off is. Each point should follow this pattern: state the method → explain the mechanism → explain the impact on the business. For 9-mark Analyse in Context questions, embedding specific details from the scenario is what separates Mastering answers from Developing ones. Naming the business or its sector once is not enough — you must weave contextual details (location, size, type of vacancy) into your analysis at least twice to score in the upper tier.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A job description details the role and its duties; a person specification details the qualities the ideal candidate must have. Both documents guide the recruitment process before a single application is received.
  • Internal recruitment is faster and cheaper and motivates existing staff; external recruitment brings new skills and perspectives but costs more. The right choice depends on the vacancy, the urgency, and the skills available internally.
  • Training — whether formal, informal, or through performance reviews — raises productivity, builds motivation, and improves retention by showing employees the business is invested in their future.

practice_questions.marks: A document that describes the skills, qualifications, experience and personal qualities required of a successful candidate. [1 mark — accept any accurate definition capturing the distinction between 'person' and 'job description'.]

practice_questions.text: Outline one advantage and one disadvantage of using internal recruitment.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantage (1 mark identification + 1 mark development in context):
• Internal recruitment is cheaper because the business does not need to spend on external advertising or agency fees. [1+1]

Disadvantage (1 mark):
• Promoting internally leaves a vacancy elsewhere in the business, which may create a secondary recruitment problem. [1]
[3 marks total. Accept other valid points.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a growing business should invest in formal training for its employees.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark the best two points only. Up to 3 marks per point.

Point 1 example:
• Formal training improves employee productivity. [1] When employees develop new skills through structured courses or workshops, they can carry out tasks more accurately and efficiently. [+1] This directly reduces costs through fewer mistakes and faster output, contributing to higher profit margins for the business. [+1]

Point 2 example:
• Formal training improves employee retention. [1] Employees who see the business investing in their development feel valued and are less likely to look for work elsewhere. [+1] Lower staff turnover saves the business the significant cost of repeatedly recruiting and inducting new employees. [+1]

Other creditable points: retraining for new technology; improved quality of customer service; motivation through skill development.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Sandton Brew is an independent craft brewery in Sheffield, founded by Maya Sandhu five years ago. The business has grown from 6 to 34 employees and recently expanded into distributing to regional supermarkets. Maya now needs to hire a distribution manager. She currently has no one internally with logistics experience, but promoting from within has always been her preference because staff morale is high and she values loyalty.

Analyse the impact on Sandton Brew of recruiting the distribution manager externally rather than internally.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Sustained analysis of the impact of external recruitment in the context of Sandton Brew specifically. The answer examines the benefit of bringing in logistics expertise that does not currently exist internally, analyses the impact on cost and time (external advertising, interviewing, induction), and considers the potential effect on existing staff morale given Maya's culture of internal promotion. The analysis acknowledges trade-offs and reaches a supported judgement about the overall impact.

Secure (5–7 marks): The answer develops at least two impacts of external recruitment (e.g. new expertise vs higher cost), with reference to Sandton Brew's context. Some analysis of the morale or culture dimension. A conclusion or overall judgement is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): At least one impact identified with basic development. Some reference to the scenario, but context may be superficial.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple statements about internal or external recruitment with little or no reference to the case.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'A business should always prioritise external recruitment over internal recruitment when filling senior vacancies.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues the case for external recruitment at senior level (fresh strategic thinking, specialist skills not available internally, avoidance of internal politics) AND challenges the statement with strong counter-arguments (cost; risk of cultural disruption; loss of motivation for internal candidates who were passed over; internal candidates understand the business). The conclusion adds new evaluative thinking — for example, that the right approach depends on the nature of the vacancy, whether the business is in a growth or stability phase, and the current depth of internal talent. Conclusion does not simply restate prior points.

Secure (7–9 marks): Arguments for and against the statement with development, some use of business concepts (e.g. retention, morale, cost). A conclusion is reached but may not add fully new evaluative thinking.

Developing (4–6 marks): Some arguments on both sides, partially developed. Conclusion present but limited.

Emerging (1–3 marks): One-sided or undeveloped points. Little or no conclusion.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Identify two documents a business uses when recruiting for a new role.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Job description
• Person specification
• Application form
[2 marks. Do not accept CV — that is prepared by the applicant, not the business.]

knowledge_checks.q: What does a person specification describe?
options: The duties and responsibilities of the job role
The qualifications and qualities required of the ideal candidate
The salary and benefits offered to the successful applicant
The number of employees in the department

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an advantage of internal recruitment?
options: It always brings new skills into the business
It removes the need for a job description
It is typically faster and cheaper than external recruitment
It guarantees a higher standard of candidate

knowledge_checks.q: A _____ is a document prepared by the applicant summarising their education, qualifications and work experience.
There is a strong link between training, motivation and _____ — employees who develop their skills are more likely to stay with the business.
Match each recruitment or training term to its correct description:
right: A document listing the duties and responsibilities of a role
Structured, planned learning delivered in a session or course
A regular meeting between manager and employee to review progress and targets

flashcard_questions.a: A document that outlines the responsibilities and duties expected of the person filling a specific role.
A document describing the skills, qualifications and qualities required of the ideal candidate.

flashcard_questions.q: Which document does the applicant prepare themselves — job description, CV or application form?
Give one advantage of internal recruitment over external recruitment.
flashcard_questions.a: Faster and cheaper — no external advertising costs and the candidate already knows the business.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one disadvantage of internal recruitment.
flashcard_questions.a: It leaves a vacancy elsewhere in the business and brings in no new ideas.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of external recruitment.
flashcard_questions.a: Brings in fresh skills, perspectives and expertise the business does not currently have.
Structured, planned training delivered by an employer or provider, often in a session or course.
Unstructured learning through day-to-day work, such as watching experienced colleagues.
A regular meeting between manager and employee to review targets and discuss development needs.

flashcard_questions.q: What is retention in a business context?
flashcard_questions.a: A business's ability to keep its employees over time, reducing costly staff turnover.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does high staff retention benefit a business?
flashcard_questions.a: It saves the time and money involved in repeatedly recruiting, selecting and onboarding new staff.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a business retrain existing employees?
flashcard_questions.a: To ensure they can use new technology safely and efficiently after an upgrade.

flashcard_questions.q: Which job role sits at the top of a business hierarchy, setting strategy and direction?
What role do supervisors play in the organisational hierarchy?
flashcard_questions.a: They manage front-line staff directly, monitoring day-to-day performance.

glossary_terms.definition: A document that describes the tasks, duties and responsibilities of a job role.
A document that describes the skills, qualifications, experience and personal qualities required of a successful candidate.
A form provided by the employer for applicants to fill in with personal details, qualifications and experience.
A document prepared by the applicant summarising their personal details, education, qualifications and work experience.
Senior leaders responsible for the strategic direction and overall performance of the business, accountable to shareholders.
Middle-level managers who oversee teams of operational staff, monitor day-to-day performance, and act as a link between senior management and front-line employees.
Filling a vacancy by promoting or moving an existing employee within the business.
Filling a vacancy by advertising to people outside the business.
Structured, planned training delivered by an employer or provider, often in a classroom or dedicated training session.
Unstructured learning that happens naturally through day-to-day work, such as learning by watching colleagues or asking questions.
A regular meeting between a manager and an employee to review progress against targets and discuss development needs.
The ability of a business to keep its employees over time, reducing costly staff turnover.

items.title: Eat Sleep Work Repeat — Why Recruitment Is Broken
items.description: Bruce Daisley examines how traditional hiring processes fail to find the best people and what progressive businesses are doing differently — links internal vs external debates.

items.title: The Bottom Line — Training and Retention
items.description: Evan Davis leads a panel discussing why training is one of the highest-return investments a business can make, and how poor retention destroys profitability.

items.title: The Surprising Habits of Original Thinkers — Adam Grant
items.description: TED talk on what makes people genuinely creative and effective employees — a different take on what good recruitment should look for beyond qualifications on a person specification.

items.title: Building a Psychologically Safe Workplace — Amy Edmondson
items.description: TEDx talk on how training and development cultures that allow mistakes actually accelerate learning and performance — directly connects formal training to retention and productivity.

items.title: The Internship (2013)
items.description: Two older workers navigate Google's unconventional recruitment and training process — a light-hearted exploration of why person specifications alone don't predict performance.

items.title: The Apprentice UK (TV Show)
items.description: Candidates compete through recruitment-style tasks that test skills, interview performance and cultural fit — showing exactly what employers look for beyond a CV.

items.title: BBC Bitesize — Recruitment and Training
items.description: GCSE notes on job descriptions, person specifications, internal and external recruitment, and the difference between formal and informal training — with practice questions.

items.title: CIPD — Recruitment and Selection Factsheet
items.description: The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development's factsheet on UK recruitment best practice, covering job descriptions, person specs, selection methods and interview techniques.

items.description: Exam-focused revision notes on all recruitment documents, internal vs external trade-offs, training types and how they link to employee performance reviews.
